newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl says Germany to qualify for EMU on time.
newsitem.headline: Kohl says Germany to qualify for EMU on time.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Saturday that Germany would fulfil the convergence criteria for European monetary union (EMU) and the European Union's single currency would be launched as planned in 1999.

Dismissing mounting doubts that a weak economy and record post-World War Two unemployment in Germany would force government borrowing over the limits set by the Maastricht treaty, Kohl said his countrywould meet its commitments to join EMU on time.
"We will stick to both the agreed start date and the convergence criteria," he said in a speech to delegates to a tourism fair in Berlin.
He added that the euro must be a stable and strong. He said the currency would become reality despite all forecasts to the contrary.
Kohl was speaking after the government's top independent economic adviser was quoted as saying Germany would in all likelihood miss Maastricht's budget deficit and national debt goals this year.
Herbert Hax, head of the "five wise men" economic advisory panel, urged Germany to put off joining the euro currency project until its own financial house is in order.
"The truth is quite simple: Stability comes before the timetable," Hax told the weekly newspaper Bild am Sonntag.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel has pledged to cut the budget deficit this year to below the Maastricht goal of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
Meeting the goal would enable European Union leaders to give Germany the green light next year to join the start of EMU in 1999. But Hax said that would be tough.
"The government forecast is 2.9 percent, but there are others who predict over three percent," he told Bild am Sonntag in remarks released in advance of Sunday publication.
"If you take the stability criteria seriously, Germany will probably not be able to introduce the euro as planned in 1999."
He also said Germany would probably overstep the EMU public debt target of 60 percent of GDP in 1997.

Hax's comments carry weight because the forecasts of the wise men underpin government budget planning. The group last November forecast a deficit this year of 3.3 percent of GDP, down from a final 3.8 percent in 1996.

Waigel's budget assumes economic growth of 2.5 percent -- but that forecast received a blow on Saturday after another of Germany's leading economic institutes was reported to have knocked a half-percentage point off its GDP growth forecast to two percent.

News magazine Focus said the IWH institute in Halle had cut its forecast because the German economy had stagnated in late 1996. The IWH forecast a jobless rate for 1997 of 11 percent of the workforce, or more than 4.2 million people without work -- up from 10.4 percent previously.
The IWH is the second top think-tank to cut its forecast to two percent. But a third, the Kiel-based IfW institute said on Saturday it expected the government forecast to be met.
That will not be enough, however, to reduce the 1997 budget deficit, which the IfW forecast at 3.5 percent of GDP.
Although dole queues are likely to shorten from February's 4.7 million this spring, lower tax revenues and extra jobless costs are already tipping the fiscal arithmetic against Waigel.
Hax said Germany and the EU must make it clear now whether they intend to make use of the leeway offered by Maastricht or to put off EMU until state finances are in better shape.

"Either you loosen the criteria, and you have to say so now, or Germany will have to get ready for the euro later," he said. "Unfortunately, the politicians have turned the possibility of a delay into a taboo."
He added: "Germany and a group of other countries will probably not fulfil the convergence criteria before 1998. Only after that can the euro be introduced in all these countries."
That would mean that the euro would be launched in 2000. "That would be better than if four or five countries march ahead," Hax said.
